name: David Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing adult nursing, so my week is half lectures and half skills labs where we practise on dummies. Tuesday is anatomy at nine and I'm usually in the library after, writing notes by hand because I remember them better. I share a flat with three lads from my course near the campus. Mum and Dad pay for everything, which I'm grateful for, and on Sundays I still go home to Coventry for dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honestly, because people keep telling me AI will replace everyone and I don't buy it. If it's hype, then my course is safe and nurses still matter. I'd probably say it in the flat group chat with a bit of smugness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd feel relieved but also a bit angry at the tech bosses who made everyone panic for money. My Dad drives a bus and his union rep told him the same hype happened with driverless buses. I don't think it changes much for nursing in the next four years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep going to placements, keep handwriting my notes, and carry on saving a bit from my allowance. I might sign up to the students' union nursing society, because the older nurses on placement say staffing is the real problem, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I'm one of the lucky ones with parents who pay, so money isn't a worry. The only thing on my mind is whether the ward staffing will be bad when I qualify, but that was true before AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said staffing is the real problem. What did you see on placement that made you say that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I spent two days on a medical ward where one nurse had eleven patients, and the nurse still held a man's hand when he was scared. No software is doing that. If anything goes wrong, it will be because the hospital trust won't hire enough people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools at all, even for study?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I don't plan to. I don't trust where the answers come from, and my tutor said it can make up references. I'd rather read the textbook myself, even if it's slower. My flatmate Tariq uses it for essays and I tell him he's lazy, but kindly.

say: I'd say **hype** is making people scared for no reason, and nursing is safe.
I'd tell my flatmates the **tech bosses** are selling fear to sell products.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, though I'm a bit angry at the people who started the panic.
I think the real danger to nursing is **short staffing**, not software.
do: Keep **handwriting notes** and going to placements exactly as I do now.
Join the students' union **nursing society** to push on ward staffing.
feel: I feel **calm**, helped by parents who pay for everything.
S0.quote: I spent two days on a medical ward where one nurse had eleven patients, and the nurse still held a man's hand when he was scared.
fieldNote: Resistant to **AI tools** but not anxious; his certainty comes from placement experience on a real ward.
Blames employers and **tech bosses**, in line with his union-family upbringing.
Money is no pressure at all, which keeps his mood **calm**.

steps.text: Keep handwriting notes and attending every placement shift
Join the students' union nursing society this term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming for desk jobs first, so people in offices should get organised. Nursing has a lot of paperwork, so I'd say software might take the forms and leave the patients to us. I'd say it to my Dad's union friends, who'd agree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my job survives but the hospital changes. Software will do the rota, the notes and the booking, and the trust might use that to cut admin staff and push more onto nurses. I worry the managers will call it efficiency and give us more patients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally learn what the ward systems do, because I'd be forced to. Maybe not AI by choice, but I'd learn the hospital's own software on placement. I'd also go to a union meeting at the hospital in second year and ask what they're doing about workloads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. I'm not afraid for my job, but I'm afraid of being told to do more with the same number of people. It feels like something that gets decided above my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be forced to learn it. Does that sit alright with you, given you avoid AI tools now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a fair point. I avoid it by choice, but a ward isn't my choice, it's the trust's. If the notes system needs me to dictate into it, I'll dictate into it. What I won't do is trust it blindly, I'll check what it wrote about my patient.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want a union to ask for in that situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A promise in writing that the time saved goes back to patients, not into cutting posts. My Dad's union got that kind of clause after the bus company introduced ticket machines. If tools save an hour per shift, I want that hour spent at the bedside.

say: I'd say software takes the **paperwork** and nurses should keep the patients.
I'd warn friends that **desk jobs** go first and people should organise.
think: I worry managers will call it **efficiency** and give nurses more patients.
I think my job survives, but the **ward** changes around me.
do: Learn the hospital's **notes system** on placement, even though I avoid AI by choice.
Go to a **union meeting** in second year and ask about workloads.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, because it's decided above my head.
S1.quote: If tools save an hour per shift, I want that hour spent at the bedside.
fieldNote: Reasoning comes straight from his father's **bus union** experience with ticket machines and a written promise.
Keeps his opposition to AI personal but accepts **workplace systems** he is told to use.
Fears **workload**, not job loss, which is a mild and specific worry.

steps.text: Learn the ward's notes software during placement shifts
Attend a hospital union meeting in second year
Keep studying nursing and ask tutors about workload

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready and that governments have been asleep. I'd say it loudly, online and in the students' union. Someone has to decide who owns the machines, and it can't be four companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it scares me. Within two years I'm barely into my second year, and everything I know about office work being taken makes me think the money gets pulled out of the NHS tax base. Nursing might be fine for the hands-on part until 2031, but I don't know if there will be funding for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on my course because patients still need people. I'd go home and talk with Mum and Dad about what the family does if Dad's bus company goes driverless, because that's his job. And I'd get involved in protests about public ownership, properly, not just sharing posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and a bit angry. I can see that my own job might be fine for a while, but my parents' work and the hospital's money are not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your parents' jobs worries you most, and why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's, definitely. My dad is fifty-one and has driven buses for twenty years, and if robots drive the bus, he has no other trade. Mum works as a pharmacy assistant, and that is mostly counter work with chatting. But Dad would be out and I'd have to think about helping with money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had two years only, how does that change your degree plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still finish. A nursing degree is a registration, a licence, and the hospital can't hand that to a chatbot easily. But I might drop my idea of a master's, and look for paid shifts as a healthcare assistant in the holidays so I can send some money home.

say: I'd say governments are **asleep** and the machines can't be owned by four companies.
I'd push for **public ownership** online and in the students' union.
think: I'm scared that **funding** for the NHS collapses even if nursing stays safe.
I worry most about **Dad's** bus job, which is all he knows.
do: Stay on the **nursing course**, since registration is a licence AI can't give.
Take **healthcare assistant** shifts in the holidays to send money home.
feel: I feel **anxious** and angry, mostly for my parents.
S2.quote: My dad is fifty-one and has driven buses for twenty years, and if robots drive the bus, he has no other trade.
fieldNote: His own job feels safer than his father's; the **anxiety** is about his household.
Political reflex is **public ownership** and unions.
Parents' money is the cushion, so the worry is the cushion itself going.

steps.text: Take healthcare assistant shifts during the holidays
Join the public ownership campaign in the students' union
Sit down with Mum and Dad to plan for Dad's bus job going
Go on the next union march with the nursing society

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for a plan if we start now. I'd say it in the nursing society: we should be lobbying for retraining funds and a short working week. I'd want people to treat it as an election issue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, five years means I'm just qualifying in 2029 and starting my first ward job when everything is wobbling. I think hospitals are the last place to change, so I'd have a job, but the pay and the staffing could be uncertain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work as a nurse, and vote for any party that puts money into retraining. I'd also keep up with Dad's union, which says they'll push for a four-day week. And I'd try to learn a little about the systems, because older nurses said the patients ask about them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More uneasy than anxious. There's time, and I'm in a job where people still need hands. But I think about the people in my family who don't have that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lobby for a short working week. How would that actually work in a hospital?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't fully know. Hospitals run around the clock, so a shorter week means more nurses, not fewer hours covered. But if the machines do the paperwork, maybe the same twelve-hour shift could be a ten-hour shift, with the same pay. I'd put that to the union and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger cousin who is thinking of a computing degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Imran to pick something with people in it, because coding is exactly what the AI takes first. He's fifteen and wants to code, so I'd say I'd tell him to do it as a skill and study something like physio or nursing as the main thing.

say: I'd say five years is **enough time** if we lobby for retraining funds now.
I'd call for a **shorter working week** at the nursing society.
think: I expect to qualify in 2029 into a **wobbly** system, but with a job.
I think hospitals change **last**, so I'm safer than most.
do: Finish the degree and **vote** for parties that fund retraining.
Back my Dad's union push for a **four-day week**.
feel: I feel **uneasy** but not afraid, with time to act.
S3.quote: I'd tell my cousin Imran to pick something with people in it, because coding is exactly what the AI takes first.
fieldNote: Time lowers his temperature; he converts worry into **political activity**.
Advice to his cousin shows how he reads **exposure** in different careers.
Still a resistant user, but practical about learning hospital systems.

steps.text: Vote for parties promising retraining funds
Finish the nursing degree and register in 2029
Learn the ward software on placements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's call this one "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at uni, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and we shouldn't waste it on panic. I'd tell friends to enjoy their degrees and keep an eye on the politics. Plenty can change in ten years, including who is in government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd be a qualified nurse for about seven of those years, and then the hands-on robots come around 2039 when I'm thirty-two. I'd probably be in charge of a ward by then, so I'd be the one managing the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, work on a ward, and maybe do a leadership course so I'm on the side of staff when the decisions get made. I'd also save my wages properly, because I've never had to. And I'd stay in the union all the way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. A decade is time to build a career and have a say. It's the two-year one that scares me, not this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years that you couldn't in the shorter versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get to be useful. With two years I can only panic, but with ten I can become a ward sister or charge nurse and sit in the meetings where the trust decides how to use new tools. I want to be in that room, arguing for staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned saving your wages. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I spend my allowance on takeaways and football tickets. In ten years I'd be paying rent, so I'd put away maybe two hundred a month from my first job into a plain savings account. Not shares, I don't trust those, just a cushion for when it gets strange.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long enough to avoid panic and watch the politics.
I'd tell friends to **enjoy** their degrees.
think: I'd probably be **running a ward** when hands-on robots arrive, managing the change.
I think a decade lets me become someone in the **room** where tools are chosen.
do: Qualify, work on a ward and take a **leadership course** to represent staff.
Save about **two hundred** a month from my first job in a plain account.
feel: I feel **calm**, with time to build a career.
S4.quote: With two years I can only panic, but with ten I can become a ward sister or charge nurse
fieldNote: Time converts anxiety into **ambition** and union-minded leadership.
Admits he has never had to save; his cushion has been his **parents**.

steps.text: Qualify as a nurse and work on a medical ward
Take a nurse leadership course after two years on the ward
Save two hundred a month in a plain savings account
Stay in the union and stand as a ward rep

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. It's too quick for my parents, my hospital or any government to react, and Dad's job would be the first to go. What would help is a real plan before it arrives: public money for retraining, strong unions at the table and a rule that productivity gains get shared.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not as against technology as I sound. I'm against it being run by a handful of companies with no say for workers. If it's regulated and the benefits are shared, I'd be happy for a robot to carry the laundry so I can sit with a patient.

headlineQuote: I'm not as against technology as I sound. I'm against it being run by a handful of companies with no say for workers.
portrait: David is a 19-year-old **nursing** student from Coventry whose parents pay for everything.
He avoids **AI tools** by choice and writes notes by hand, though he'd accept hospital software.
His **union** background shapes him: he blames tech bosses and wants public ownership and regulation.
He feels **calm** about his own job because nursing is hands-on, but anxious for his father's bus job.
More time turns his worry into a plan: qualify, lead a ward and speak for staff.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, because his parents and the NHS can't prepare in two years.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **public money** for retraining, strong unions and a rule that productivity gains are shared.
